query: FeNiCrCoCu is considered suitable for thin-film use, and its expense favors applying it as a protective coating on conventional metals rather than using it in bulk. Earlier studies examined room-temperature wear behavior in relation to coating–substrate combinations, composition, and grain size, but largely addressed the alloy itself or a limited thermal regime rather than the overall wear response of a coating across different temperatures. Under the constraints that FeNiCrCoCu remains a thin protective coating and that high-temperature wear is the target application, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its overall wear resistance and why? Specify an intervention relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the observations expected if the hypothesis is correct, state the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, connect the hypothesis to prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The wear resistance of FeNiCrCoCu thin-film protective coatings at elevated temperatures is governed by the formation of a protective oxide layer, which is enhanced by the high-entropy effect and the presence of Cr, and can be optimized by controlling the coating's microstructure and composition.
generation.material_initial_state: FeNiCrCoCu thin-film protective coating on conventional metals
generation.intervention: In-situ transmission electron microscopy (TEM) or scanning electron microscopy (SEM) to study wear-induced microstructural changes at elevated temperatures
generation.conditions: Elevated temperatures (up to 900°C) and various loading conditions
generation.mechanism: High-entropy effect and Cr presence enhancing oxide layer formation
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved wear resistance by 20% compared to baseline coating condition
generation.baseline: FeNiCrCoCu thin-film protective coating without optimized microstructure and composition
generation.boundary: Temperature range: 25°C to 900°C, loading range: 10 MPa to 100 MPa
generation.uncertainty: The exact mechanism of protective oxide layer formation and its relationship with the high-entropy effect and Cr presence is not fully understood and requires further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Wear testing of FeNiCrCoCu thin-film protective coatings at elevated temperatures with varying microstructure and composition
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the wear resistance of the coating does not improve by at least 15% compared to the baseline condition, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) first appeared in public view in 2010 [ [1] ]. Thereafter, they aroused great concern from researchers at home and abroad. Research has proved that RHEAs have excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures, even surpassing the widely used nickel-based alloy [ [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. RHEAs, with excellent mechanical properties at elevated temperatures, are considered promising high-temperature application materials, which are suitable for complex working conditions such as atomic energy, aerospace, the military industry, advanced nuclear reactors, etc. Previous studies focused on mechanical properties at high- and room-temperatures, but with little research and analysis on high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [7] , [8] , [9] ]. The research shows that adding the proper amount of Al, Cr, and Si elements into the refractory high-entropy alloy can form a dense oxidation film on the surface of the alloy in a high-temperature environment, thus improving the high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [10] , [11] , [12] , [13] ]. This paper utilizes in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) to investigate the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). We found that (1) Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn; (2) no oxides like Cr 2 O 3 , Fe 2 O 3 , or Fe 3 O 4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi, which contradicts some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. We also analysed and compared the experimental results with thermodynamic calculations by using ThermoCalc version 2022b software following the CALPHAD method. ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results; also, in an atmospheric environment, it predicted only spinel, indicating the need for further investigation into factors to validate the thermodynamic predictions.
